newsitem.title: IRAN: Iranian parliament to vet Khatami cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Iranian parliament to vet Khatami cabinet.

text.p: Iran's parliament begins the task of vetting President Mohammad Khatami's proposed cabinet on Tuesday.

Khatami, a moderate 54-year-old Shi'ite Moslem cleric, is expected to lose at least one of his 22 cabinet nominees at the hands of conservatives and hardline radicals in the 270-seat Majlis, or parliament, newspapers and analysts say.
The conservative-led assembly is expected to start the first of three five-hour debates on the cabinet nominees at 8:00 a.m. (0330 GMT) on Tuesday. A final vote is expected on Wednesday.

"Everything is possible. However, it is not possible to predict which of them will get the vote of confidence and who will not," parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri told the official news agency IRNA on Monday.

Some of the proposed ministers are expected to go to parliament to argue their case on Wednesday though Iranian newspapers have reported that nominees have been lobbying hard in the corridors of parliament to secure votes.
A source at the president's office said it was not yet clear whether Khatami would go to the assembly during its debates.
The final make-up of the cabinet is seen as crucial in setting the reforming tone of Khatami's four-year term.

Khatami was swept into power during national elections in May after scooping the votes of Iranian youth, women and the middle class who saw him as a leader able to inject social and economic freedoms into the 18-year-old Islamic Republic.
He was sworn into office on August 4.

Despite the expected loss of at least one minister nominated to a sensitive domestic portfolio, Khatami will emerge with the majority of his cabinet largely intact and his election mandate for change undamaged, analysts said.

"There is a consensus among the deputies that the majority of the proposed ministers will get the vote of confidence," influential conservative deputy Mohammad Reza Bahonar told the newspaper Resalat on Monday.
Khatami would circumvent the rejection of some candidates by appointing them as vice presidents who would then assume de facto charge of ministeries, the daily Iran News said.

"If any of President Khatami's proposed ministers are rejected by the Majlis, the President will then appoint the rejected minister, or ministers, as (a) vice president," it said. Vice presidents do not need to be approved by parliament.

Khatami has said that vice presidents are members of the cabinet in addition to the 22 portfolios. Analysts said it was likely that he would appoint vice presidents for youth affairs and women's issues.
Strong opposition is expected from conservative factions in parliament to Khatami's proposed culture minister Ataollah Mohajerani and interior minister Abdollah Nouri.

"Opponents try to weaken President Khatami's cabinet so that after a while they can claim that the cabinet is not functioning," Faezeh Hashemi, parliament deputy and daughter of former president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, was quoted as saying by the daily Akhbar.

The Culture Ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami's supporters who want to introduce more freedoms and conservatives who see it as the main weapon against "Western cultural invasion".
The ministry has power over what books, films and music are allowed in the country.
Mohajerani has become a lightning rod for conservatives and hardliners for his support in 1990 of a resumption of talks with the United States.
"If such a person takes over the Ministry of Guidance (culture), the cultural independence of the country will be damaged," parliament deputy Jahanbakhsh Mohebbi, told Resalat on Sunday.
The Interior Ministry has influence over the conduct of elections and the appointment of provincial governors.
Ultimate power, particularly in foreign relations, in this country of 60 million people rests firmly in the hands of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
